The ACM would find the firmware's initial boot block no longer verifies against the OEM key, and the policy would stop the boot
Nothing, Boot Guard only measures
The TPM would erase the implant
explain: ESET states that with Boot Guard available and properly configured, the machine would have refused to boot after the compromise. Secure Boot, which runs inside the modified firmware, would not.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Firmware updates, resilience and the BMC beside the CPU
question: A firmware update tool verifies the vendor's signature but accepts any signed version. Which NIST SP 800-147 recommendation does it miss?
options: Secure local update
Rollback prevention: refusing authentic but older images with known weaknesses
Non-bypassability
None
explain: 800-147 says the authenticated update mechanism should prevent rollback to an earlier authentic version with a known security weakness, for example by comparing version numbers.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3: producer and consumer warps, then ping-pong
question: A teammate proposes giving the producer warpgroup as many registers as the consumers, "to be fair." What is the most likely effect?
options: Faster loads, because TMA needs registers for each byte copied
No effect, because register counts are fixed per kernel
Fewer registers for the consumers, forcing smaller tiles or spills in the math path
Better ping-pong, because both warpgroups can then do softmax
explain: TMA is issued by a single thread and copies data without staging it in registers. Registers given to the producer are taken from the consumers, which hold the accumulators; the paper deallocates producer registers and reallocates them to consumers for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, determinism and scheduling
question: A varlen inference batch contains short prefills followed by a few very long-context decodes. Which FlashAttention-4 scheduling idea addresses the resulting slowdown?
options: Conditional softmax rescaling
Sorting batches by their per-tile cost so the longest work starts first (LPT)
Emulating the exponential on FMA units
Switching to FP8
explain: This is load imbalance: if long work is processed last, a few SMs finish late while others sit idle. The paper launches a small preprocessing kernel to sort batches by cost and write a virtual-to-actual batch index map, which can be cached so sorting costs nothing on later calls.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Load-balanced scheduling, plan and run, and CUDA graphs
question: An engine calls plan() before every layer's run() in a 32-layer model. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, plan must precede every run
plan() must be called only once at startup
run() will use the wrong KV pages
It repeats identical CPU scheduling 32 times per step, since all layers share the same lengths
explain: The plan depends only on the sequence lengths and page arrays, which are the same for every layer in a step. The docs and paper design plan for reuse across all layers; calling it per layer adds CPU overhead to every step. Calling it only at startup is also wrong, because lengths change every step.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Generating data by following a velocity field from noise
question: Why was maximum-likelihood training of continuous normalizing flows expensive compared with flow matching?
options: The loss required simulating the ODE (and backpropagating through it) on every training step
The network had to output a full probability density instead of a velocity
Maximum likelihood cannot be used with Gaussian noise
It needed a discriminator network as in a GAN
explain: Likelihood training of a CNF integrates the ODE inside the training loop. Flow matching regresses the network onto a closed-form target velocity at a sampled point, so no simulation happens during training.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Relation to diffusion, and rectified flow in Stable Diffusion 3
question: Which statement best describes the relation between diffusion models and flow matching?
options: They are unrelated; diffusion requires an SDE and cannot be sampled with an ODE
Diffusion paths are Gaussian conditional paths within the flow matching framework, and diffusion models can be sampled with the probability flow ODE
Flow matching is a special case of DDPM with a different noise schedule
Flow matching can only learn straight paths, diffusion can learn curved ones
explain: Lipman et al. recover VE and VP diffusion paths as Gaussian conditional paths, and Song et al.'s probability flow ODE gives diffusion models a deterministic sampler. The marginal flow of any of these, including OT paths, can be curved.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
question: In the TLAPS proof, which assumption lets the same proof cover 3, 5 or 1,001 acceptors?
options: AllowRestart = FALSE
Any two quorums intersect
Values has exactly two elements
TypeOK
explain: Step <1>3 needs one acceptor in both quorums, and QuorumsMeet supplies it for any size. NoRestart is needed too, but it is about the environment, not the size. The proof never mentions how many acceptors or values exist.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Ghost permissions, VerusSync and what a proof trusts
question: A Verus project verifies cleanly, yet in production the service corrupts data. Which explanation is NOT possible if Verus and Z3 are sound?
options: The top-level ensures clause did not state the property that matters
The verified exec function returned a value violating its ensures clause on some input
A trusted spec of an external crate was wrong
The code contains assume(...) that is false
explain: If the tools are sound and nothing false is assumed, every verified function satisfies its ensures on every input. Failures come from what was assumed or trusted, or from specs that say the wrong thing.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
question: An FP8 GEMM with K = 8192 shows growing error versus a BF16 reference, even though inputs are well scaled. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The scales are stale; switch to delayed scaling
Too few mantissa bits in the inputs; switch all inputs to E5M2
Limited-precision accumulation inside the tensor cores; promote partial sums to FP32 every N_C elements
The output is BF16; write it in FP8 instead
explain: The DeepSeek report traces large-K error to about 14-bit accumulation in Hopper FP8 tensor cores and fixes it by moving partial sums to FP32 on CUDA cores every 128 elements. E5M2 inputs would make precision worse, not better.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
question: A tensor has amax 10. One block's amax is 0.05. What is that block's ideal scale before E4M3 rounding, in the stored (multiplied) form?
options: 448, like every block
explain: First s_enc = 6 x 448 / 10 = 268.8. The block's decode scale is 0.05 / 6 = 0.00833, and the stored value is 0.00833 x 268.8 = 2.24, comfortably inside E4M3's range. Without the tensor scale, 0.0083 would sit in E4M3's subnormal region.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Abuse economics: make every attempt cost more than it earns
question: A new rule cuts fraud losses by USD 8,000 a month. It also declines orders from honest customers worth USD 30,000 in profit a month. What is the right reading?
options: Ship it: fraud is down
Ship it, because declined customers will retry
It cannot be judged without the attacker's costs
Do not ship it as is: total cost went up by USD 22,000 a month
explain: The defender minimises fraud loss plus friction plus operations. Here friction rose by 30,000 while fraud fell by 8,000. Some declined customers will retry, but you must measure that, not assume it.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviour and velocity: counting what happens over time
question: Why does Stripe's 'hourly' velocity attribute sometimes include events from up to 65 minutes ago?
options: It uses 5-minute buckets, so the window is the last hour plus the current partial bucket
Clock skew between data centres
It deliberately adds random noise
Events are delivered late by card networks
explain: Bucketing trades precision for memory: a window of whole buckets plus the current one can stretch to 3,900 seconds, as Stripe's rules reference states.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Promotion and referral abuse: multi-accounting and holds
question: Why does a reward hold of about 120 days help against referrals that use stolen cards?
options: Fraudsters lose interest after a month
Banks delete card data after 120 days
It is a legal requirement
Card networks typically allow disputes within 120 days, so most stolen-card payments are disputed before the reward would be paid
explain: The hold covers the period in which the real cardholder typically disputes the charge. The dispute then cancels the pending reward, so the attacker's value per success drops toward zero.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Chargebacks, disputes and the true cost of a fraudulent order
question: A model is retrained every Monday on all orders up to the previous Sunday, using 'has a fraud chargeback' as the label. What bias does this create?
options: None, chargebacks are exact
Recent orders are labelled good because their disputes have not arrived, so the model underestimates fraud in fresh patterns
The model will overestimate fraud on old orders
It only affects debit cards
explain: Disputes typically arrive over up to 120 days or more. Train on orders old enough for labels to mature, or model label delay explicitly.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Enforcement, explanations and appeals
question: Which statement of reasons best balances the user's right to understand with not teaching attackers?
options: 'Your account violated our policies.'
'Blocked: risk score 0.91 > threshold 0.85 from features device_cards_1h=6, ip_type=hosting.'
'Suspended for 30 days under Payments policy 3.2 (use of payment cards that are not yours): 6 different cards were added to your account on 3 Nov and declined. You can appeal here.'
No message; silent bans prevent evasion
explain: It names the policy and the observed behaviour and gives an appeal route, without exposing the score threshold or feature names an attacker could tune against. The first says nothing useful; the second leaks the detector.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Group commit: one WAL flush makes many transactions durable
question: A WAL device needs 4 ms per flush and is busy flushing all the time. On average each flush carries 10 commit records. What is the commit throughput?
options: 250 commits/s
2,500 commits/s
40 commits/s
25,000 commits/s
explain: X = B / F = 10 / 0.004 s = 2,500 commits/s. Without sharing (B = 1) the same device tops out at 250/s.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Fuzzing from a stormy night in 1988: random, mutation, generation
question: What did Miller's original fuzz study use as its oracle?
options: A specification of each utility's correct output
Code coverage reached by each input
A comparison with a second implementation
Whether the program crashed or hung
explain: The oracle was deliberately simple: crash or hang means fail. That is why it could be automated across many programs and operating systems with no model of what each program should do.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Sanitizers as oracles: which bug each one catches
question: The TSan run printed hits = 200000, the correct total. Why is the report still a real bug?
options: It is not; the output proves the code is correct
TSan always reports false positives on counters
The total is only correct because of TSan
A race is undefined behaviour; this run got lucky, other compilers, optimisation levels or timings can lose updates
explain: TSan reports the unsynchronised access itself, not a wrong answer. Correct output on one run proves nothing about the next one, which is exactly why a race detector beats checking results.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Continuous fuzzing at scale: OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzz and Heartbleed
question: How was Cloudbleed actually discovered?
options: A fuzzer crashed Cloudflare's edge servers
Cloudflare's monitoring alerted on high memory use
A customer reported a wrong page
Data gathered for fuzzing corpora contained leaked memory that did not match what Tavis Ormandy expected
explain: Ormandy's Project Zero report describes a corpus distillation project: public data collected to build fuzzing corpora contained uninitialised memory. Fuzzing infrastructure found it, but not by crashing anything.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Variant analysis and patch diffing: one bug, many siblings
question: Why did fuzzing find new Bash bugs after the first Shellshock patch?
options: The patch introduced them
AFL is better than code review at all bugs
The bugs were in a different program
The first patch only blocked one symptom; the function-import parser, still reachable from untrusted environment variables, had more bugs that AFL's coverage feedback explored
explain: Zalewski's write-up: AFL derived about 1,000 distinct test cases from one seed function definition and found CVE-2014-6277 and 6278 in the same parser. The robust fix stopped untrusted variables from reaching it.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
question: You only accept matches with at most 1 edit. The query has 6 characters and a candidate has 9. How much of the DP table must you fill to reject the candidate?
options: All 7 x 10 cells
Only the diagonal band of width 3
None: the length difference already proves the distance is at least 3
Only the last row
explain: Every character of length difference needs at least one insertion or deletion, so $d \ge 9-6 = 3 > 1$. A length check is the cheapest filter of all and real implementations apply it before touching the table.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
question: SymSpell with k = 1 finds that the query and a dictionary word share a one-character delete, while neither is a delete of the other. What kind of single error explains that?
options: An insertion in the query
A deletion in the query
A substitution or an adjacent transposition
Nothing; it is a false positive that cannot be within 1 edit
explain: A shared one-character delete fits one differing position (a substitution, like reieve from recieve and relieve) or an adjacent swap (receve from recieve and receive). It does not guarantee 1 edit: abc and bca share the delete bc but are 2 edits apart, so SymSpell verifies every candidate with a real distance.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Searching code space: kd-trees, tolerance and why quads beat triangles
question: Why did quint (5-star) indexes solve images more slowly than quads, even though a quint match is almost always correct?
options: 6D kd-tree lookups are impossible
The solver must try many quints before finding one whose 5 stars are all in both the image and the index, and higher-dimensional search is slower
Quint codes are not scale invariant
Quints produce more coincidental matches than triangles
explain: The paper reports that for over 80% of solved images the first quint match found was correct. The cost is elsewhere: the chance that all 5 stars are detected and catalogued is lower, so many more quints are tried, and near-neighbor search slows with dimension.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Geohash: interleave the bits, name the cell
question: Which statement about two geohashes is always true?
options: If both points share a 6-character prefix at the equator, they are at most about 1.35 km apart
If two points are less than 100 m apart, they share at least a 5-character prefix
Geohashes that are adjacent in sort order are always in adjacent cells
Two points with no shared prefix are at least 1,000 km apart
explain: A shared 6-character prefix means both points are in one cell of 1.2 km x 609.4 m, whose diagonal is about 1.35 km. The other statements fail at cell boundaries: the London pair is 69 m apart with no shared prefix, and the Z-order curve jumps between quadrants.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Pixels in memory: NHWC, NCHW, pitch and a warp's 96 bytes
question: A color-convert kernel reads an RGB8 (uchar3) NHWC image with one pixel per thread. Why is the per-instruction load efficiency about 33 percent?
options: The image rows are not padded, so the second row starts unaligned
Each channel load has stride 3 across lanes, so its sectors carry three times the bytes that one instruction uses
NHWC always loses to NCHW because planes are contiguous
A warp of 32 threads cannot cover 96 bytes in fewer than 32 transactions
explain: A uchar3 has alignment 1, so a pixel is three separate 1-byte accesses. Each of those instructions touches 32 addresses that are 3 bytes apart, spanning 96 bytes of sectors to deliver 32 useful bytes. The warp's total footprint is still contiguous, which is why the fix is a wider access (a 4-pixel carrier or an RGBA8 format), not a different layout.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Convolution: separable passes and the shared-memory halo
question: A 16x16 block computing one output per thread stages a tile for a 9x9 filter. How large is the tile, and how much of it is halo?
options: 16x16 = 256 elements, no halo, because shared memory is indexed per thread
25x25 = 625 elements, of which 369 are halo
24x24 = 576 elements, of which 320 are halo: 2.25 loads per output
32x32 = 1024 elements, rounded up to the warp size
explain: The tile is (16 + 9 - 1) square = 24x24 = 576 elements for 256 outputs, so 320 halo elements and 2.25 loads per output. The halo is k - 1 = 8 elements across both dimensions together, not k, because a radius-4 window needs 4 extra on each side.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
question: Tensor A is allocated on s0, read by a kernel on s1, then deleted without record_stream. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; the allocator always waits for all streams before reuse
The allocator raises an error because A was used on two streams
The block leaks and is never reused
s0 can reuse A's block for a new tensor while s1's kernel is still reading it
explain: Without record_stream the allocator only knows about s0. Reuse on s0 is ordered after s0's work, but nothing orders it after s1's kernel, so the new tensor can overwrite data s1 is still using.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
question: A row-major `float` matrix has `ld = 4096` columns. A kernel with 32 x 32 blocks computes `int r = blockIdx.y*32 + threadIdx.x; int c = blockIdx.x*32 + threadIdx.y;` and reads `a[r*ld + c]`. How many sectors does each warp load request?
options: 4, because the warp reads 32 floats
8, because the matrix is large
1, because all threads share c
32, because consecutive threads are 4096 floats apart
explain: Within a warp threadIdx.y is fixed and threadIdx.x runs 0 to 31, so it is r that varies. Consecutive threads are ld = 4096 floats (16 KB) apart, each in its own sector: 32 sectors per request and 12.5% efficiency. Swapping which index uses threadIdx.x fixes it.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
question: A colleague reports: "Nsight Systems says the GPU is 97 percent utilized, so the GPU is the bottleneck and we need better kernels." What is the hole in that reasoning?
options: Nothing: 97 percent time utilization means the SMs are 97 percent busy
Utilization there is time based, so a long exposed memcpy or a tiny kernel occupying one SM counts as full utilization
Nsight Systems cannot measure GPU utilization at all, only CPU time
It is wrong only if the application uses more than one CUDA stream
explain: The rule's own notes say the utilization is time utilization, not resource utilization: a single running memcpy counts the same as a huge kernel, and concurrent operations can sum past 100 percent. 97 percent busy could be 97 percent copying, or one kernel with a 1-block grid. Per-kernel counters, not timeline utilization, tell you whether the hardware is actually being used.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
question: Which single profiling decision most often invalidates a comparison between two versions of a kernel?
options: Changing the capture configuration between the two runs, for example clock, cache or replay settings
Profiling on a GPU that has a display attached
Using the basic section set instead of the full one
Reporting durations in microseconds rather than milliseconds
explain: Both the triage guide and the profiling guide insist on it: keep capture settings stable while comparing runs, and keep cache-control and replay settings identical unless the policy itself is the variable under test. A display-attached GPU adds noise and a smaller section set loses detail, but a changed control turns a measurement into an incomparable one.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Cooperating inside a block: shared memory, barriers and clusters
question: Which barrier placement is valid?
options: `if (blockIdx.x % 2 == 0) { __syncthreads(); }`
`if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0) { __syncthreads(); }`
`if (threadIdx.x < 64) { __syncthreads(); }`
`for (int k = 0; k < threadIdx.x; ++k) __syncthreads();`
explain: blockIdx.x is the same for every thread in a block, so the condition is uniform across the block and either all of its threads reach the barrier or none do. The other three depend on threadIdx, so some threads of the block skip or repeat the barrier: undefined behavior.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Finding communities: modularity and the Leiden algorithm
question: Community X has internal weight $L_X = 4$ and degree sum $k_X = 12$ in a graph with $m = 20$. What is its modularity term?
explain: $L_X/m = 4/20 = 0.20$ and $(k_X/2m)^2 = (12/40)^2 = 0.09$, so the term is 0.11. Dividing by $m$ rather than $2m$ in the second term is the common slip.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
question: FastGraphRAG builds relationships from co-occurrence instead of LLM extraction. What do you lose?
options: Community detection, which then cannot run
Relationship and entity descriptions; edges only say that two noun phrases appeared in the same text unit, so the graph is noisier
The ability to answer global questions at all
All embeddings
explain: The docs say FastGraphRAG has no entity or relationship descriptions and a noisier graph. Leiden and community reports still run, which is why it remains useful for global summary questions.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: The GRPO objective token by token: clipping, averaging and KL
question: Why does GRPO put the KL penalty in the loss rather than subtracting it from the reward like PPO for RLHF?
options: The KL in the loss is cheaper to compute
Folding a per-token KL into the reward would mix it into the group-normalized advantage, which is meant to be a pure comparison of sibling rewards
The reward cannot be negative
PPO's KL estimator is biased
explain: DeepSeekMath says adding the KL to the loss avoids complicating the advantage calculation. GRPO has no critic to spread a per-token reward over the sequence; its advantage is one standardized outcome per output.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: RLOO, GSPO, off-policy drift, and what RLVR teaches
question: A team training a large MoE model with GRPO sees token ratios swing wildly between minibatch updates even at a small learning rate, and training collapses. Which change targets that cause?
options: Raise beta so the KL term holds the policy back
Switch to sequence-level ratios and clipping (GSPO), or replay the old expert routing when recomputing ratios
Increase the group size G from 8 to 64
Divide advantages by the response length
explain: The GSPO paper traces the swings to expert routing changing after each update, so per-token ratios compare different sub-networks. Routing Replay fixes the ratios by reusing the old routing; GSPO avoids depending on per-token likelihoods at all.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
question: A consumer joins TripUpdates to the schedule using only trip_id. For a daily train with trip_id N8 departing 20:00, the producer sends an update for yesterday's N8, now running 14 hours late. What breaks?
options: Nothing, delays over 12 hours are discarded by protobuf
The feed is rejected because delay must be under 3600 s
The update cannot be applied because it has no stop_id
The update is applied to today's N8, so riders see a wrong prediction
explain: Without start_date the consumer cannot tell yesterday's instance from today's. The reference requires start_date exactly when such collisions are possible. Always key realtime state by (trip_id, start_date) and, for frequency trips, start_time.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: A 75-cent gap and the Morris worm: the 1980s internet learns
question: What made the Morris worm overload machines it had already infected?
options: It encrypted their disks
Its population control let 1 in 7 copies skip the check that should make duplicates exit, so reinfections piled up copies
It deliberately deleted system files
It sent large amounts of email spam
explain: Seeley's analysis: a test made 1 in 7 worms skip population control and become immortal. Repeated reinfection therefore multiplied processes. The worm did not encrypt or delete files.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Conficker: the botnet that made the industry organise
question: The Working Group called which outcome its biggest failure?
options: Being unable to remediate (clean) infected computers, so millions of infections remained
Missing the 1 April 2009 deadline
Failing to get ICANN involved
Failing to identify that MS08-067 was the bug
explain: The domain blocking largely worked, including for variant C, and ICANN did take part. But blocking the control channel left the infections in place on millions of machines.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: NotPetya: a wiper delivered as a software update
question: NotPetya showed a ransom note. What did Kaspersky's analysis conclude?
options: Paying the ransom always restored files
The malware only encrypted backup files
The attackers could not decrypt victims' disks even after payment, so it behaved as a wiper
It decrypted files after 30 days
explain: Kaspersky found the installation ID needed for decryption was not usable for recovery, so it was a wiper pretending to be ransomware.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
question: After a change, a service's IPC rises from 0.8 to 1.6, but requests take exactly as long as before. What is the most plausible explanation?
options: The counters are broken, since higher IPC always means faster code
The CPU clock frequency doubled
IPC is measured per core, so it cannot change per request
Cycles per request stayed the same while instructions per request doubled, for example from spinning or extra work
explain: IPC is a ratio. If time and cycles are unchanged, doubling IPC means twice as many instructions were retired per request: busy-waiting or redundant work. That is why IPC must be read alongside the raw instruction count.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
question: On a cloud VM, `perf stat` prints `<not supported>` for cycles and instructions but shows task-clock and page-faults. Why?
options: The hypervisor does not expose the hardware PMU to this guest, so only software events work
perf is too old to know these events
The program ran too briefly to count any cycles
Those events need the :u modifier
explain: task-clock and page-faults are software events maintained by the kernel. Hardware events need PMU access, which a guest only gets if the hypervisor virtualizes it.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Branchless selection and secret-independent memory access
question: You compile the mask-based ct_select and find a conditional branch in the assembly. What is the right conclusion?
options: The source is wrong; masks always compile to branches
The compiler is free to do this because C does not promise timing; use a vetted primitive or a compiler barrier and re-check
Branches are fine as long as the branch predictor is accurate
Switch to -O0, which guarantees constant time
explain: C's semantics cover results, not timing, so optimisers may reintroduce branches. Libraries use techniques such as value barriers, and you verify the output. -O0 gives no such guarantee either.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Meltdown: reading kernel memory, and why KPTI fixes it
question: Which workload should you expect to slow down most after enabling KPTI on an older CPU without PCID?
options: A numerical simulation that rarely calls the kernel
A small-message server doing many system calls per request
A GPU training job
A program that only reads from its own heap
explain: The cost is paid on every kernel entry and exit (CR3 switches and TLB flushes without PCID). System-call-heavy code pays most, as the roughly 50 percent microbenchmark slowdown shows.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Trusted hardware: TPMs, measured boot and secure enclaves
question: BitLocker seals the disk key to PCR values. An attacker replaces the bootloader with one that logs keystrokes. What happens at the next boot?
options: The TPM detects the new bootloader's signature and deletes the key
Nothing: PCRs only record the kernel
The bootloader's hash changes the PCR value, so the TPM refuses to unseal the key and recovery is needed
The attacker's bootloader can reset the PCR to the old value
explain: Extend is one-way and order-sensitive, and the first 16 PCRs reset only with the TPM. A different bootloader produces different PCRs, so the sealed key stays locked.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: CL.TE and TE.CL: two parsers, one stream
question: In a CL.TE setup, which side leaves bytes unread?
options: The back end, because chunked framing ended before the Content-Length count
The front end, because it reads Content-Length
Neither; they always agree
The client
explain: In the toy, the front end counted 13 bytes and forwarded them all; the back end's chunked parse ended after 5. The 8 bytes it never consumed sit in its buffer and prefix the next request.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: The 2025 endgame: 0.CL, Expect and upstream HTTP/1.1
question: What distinguishes a 0.CL desync from a CL.0 desync?
options: 0.CL: the front end ignores Content-Length while the back end honours it. CL.0: the front end honours it while the back end ignores it
They are two names for the same thing
0.CL only affects HTTP/2
CL.0 requires Transfer-Encoding
explain: The notation is front end first. In 0.CL the back end waits for body bytes the front end never forwarded; in CL.0 the back end leaves forwarded body bytes unread.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Poisoning with errors and with normalisation
question: Why does caching a 400 response turn one malformed request into a denial of service?
options: 400 responses are larger than 200 responses
400 responses disable TLS
The origin crashes
The error is stored under the normal key, so every later visitor receives the error instead of the page
explain: The origin is fine; the cache is now answering everyone with the stored error until it expires or is purged.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a 2 MiB mapping: offset bits, alignment, contiguity
question: A 7 MiB anonymous region starts at 0x7f0000100000, 1 MiB past a 2 MiB boundary. How many 2 MiB pages can map part of it?
options: 4, because 7 MiB rounds up to four 2 MiB pages
3, the aligned slots from 0x7f0000200000 to 0x7f0000800000
2, because both ends are misaligned
0, because the start is not aligned
explain: The region ends at 0x7f0000800000, which is aligned. The first aligned boundary inside it is 0x7f0000200000, so slots at 0x...200000, 0x...400000 and 0x...600000 are fully covered: 3 huge pages. The 1 MiB head stays on 256 small pages. A misaligned start only loses the partial slot, not the whole region.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
question: You run a 64 GiB database buffer pool on a dedicated host. It must always be backed by 2 MiB pages and must never be swapped. Which setup fits?
options: THP enabled=always with defrag=always
A hugetlb pool allocated at boot (hugepagesz=2M hugepages=N) with the database mapping it explicitly
THP madvise mode plus MADV_COLLAPSE at startup
Raise khugepaged pages_to_scan so the pool is collapsed quickly
explain: Only hugetlb gives a guarantee: pages are reserved up front, boot allocation avoids fragmentation, and hugetlb pages are not swappable. THP, including MADV_COLLAPSE, is best-effort and its pages can be swapped or split.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: How Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next stack their layers
question: Why does Nemotron-H place a Mamba-2 layer first and use no RoPE in its attention layers?
options: RoPE is incompatible with grouped-query attention
The first Mamba-2 layer is recurrent and naturally encodes position, so explicit position embeddings are not needed
Attention layers at the start would make the KV cache grow quadratically
Mamba-2 layers require RoPE inputs and must come before attention
explain: Waleffe et al. put a Mamba layer at the start so the hybrid can work without position embeddings, since the recurrence itself depends on order. Their 840M ablation also found the hybrid without RoPE did better after long-context extension (continued training on longer sequences to raise the usable context).

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer
question: A team needs exact recall of a fact stated 50,000 tokens earlier. Which design can look it up exactly rather than relying on a compressed state?
options: Griffin-style: recurrent blocks plus 2,048-token local attention
LoLCATs-style: linear attention plus a 64-token window in every layer
Zamba-style: Mamba blocks plus a shared global attention block
Pure Mamba-2 with a larger state
explain: Only the shared block attends globally: its KV cache holds all 50,000 tokens for each call. The two windowed designs can see exact tokens only within their windows, and any pure recurrent state compresses.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Choosing a fusion method and running it at scale
question: A team builds hybrid search by computing min-max normalization independently on each shard and summing there. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; min-max is a per-document operation
Shards cannot run kNN queries
Each shard uses its own min and max, so the same raw score maps to different normalized values on different shards and the merged ranking is inconsistent
It only breaks RRF, not min-max
explain: Min-max depends on the list's min and max. A shard-local list has different bounds than the global list. That is why OpenSearch normalizes after the query phase and Vespa restricts these normalizers to the global phase.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
question: A support search box must answer in 300 ms at p99 (the 99th percentile: 99 of every 100 requests must finish within 300 ms). Which HyDE plan is realistic?
options: HyDE with N=8 sequential calls
HyDE with N=8 parallel samples
Do not run HyDE on the request path; use it offline or only for a slow fallback path, and serve plain or hybrid retrieval online
Keep HyDE but drop the embedding step
explain: Even one generation is seconds in the measurements cited (over 2000 ms in query2doc, 11.58 s per query in the RAG study). Parallel sampling bounds wall time to one generation, which still breaks 300 ms. HyDE fits batch or asynchronous paths, not this budget.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic
question: A PLC reads inputs into an image table at the start of each scan. If an attacker could change the input image after it is read but before the logic runs, what would the logic do?
options: Detect the change and fault
Act on the false values as if they were real measurements
Ignore the input image and read sensors directly
Stop scanning
explain: MITRE describes the image table as what the user program uses 'instead of directly interacting with physical I/O'. Manipulating it makes correct logic act on false inputs, the essence of Stuxnet's design.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
question: Why did the replay in the scenario defeat the operator but not the safety system?
options: The safety system ignores sensors
Safety systems cannot be attacked
The replay was too slow
The SIS used its own sensor and logic, which were not on the path the attacker manipulated
explain: The replay changed what the HMI displayed. The SIS read the real level through its own transmitter and acted independently. Triton (lesson 11) shows attackers going after that last layer too, which is why its independence matters so much.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: IT/OT convergence: Colonial, Oldsmar, Unitronics, Volt Typhoon
question: Colonial's OT was not shown to be infected, yet the pipeline stopped for five days. What design lesson does CISA's advisory AA21-131A draw?
options: OT should share IT's ransomware backups
Move OT to the cloud
Pay ransoms faster
Ensure the OT network can operate at necessary capacity even if the IT network is compromised, with robust IT/OT segmentation and tested manual controls
explain: CISA and FBI urged that OT be able to keep running when IT is compromised, plus segmentation, a DMZ and regularly tested manual controls. Dependence on IT systems, not OT damage, drove the outage.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS
question: An intruder raises the high-level alarm threshold on the HMI so operators are never warned. Which ATT&CK for ICS tactic is this?
options: Collection
Discovery
Inhibit Response Function
Command and Control
explain: MITRE: in Inhibit Response Function 'the adversary is trying to prevent your safety, protection, quality assurance, and operator intervention functions from responding'. Modify Alarm Settings and Alarm Suppression are techniques under it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: SAML web SSO step by step: AuthnRequest, bindings and RelayState
question: A security review finds an SP that redirects to whatever URL arrives in RelayState after login. What is the risk?
options: None: RelayState is signed by the IdP
An open redirect: attackers can send users through a real login and then on to a phishing page
The assertion will expire
The IdP will refuse to log the user in
explain: RelayState is not covered by the assertion's signature and returns through the browser. OWASP's advice is to validate it against an allowlist when it carries a URL.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: OIDC as the modern alternative: the same job in JSON
question: Which SAML check corresponds to an OIDC relying party comparing the ID token's nonce with the value it stored before redirecting?
options: Checking AudienceRestriction
Checking InResponseTo against an AuthnRequest this session sent
Checking the Issuer
Checking SessionNotOnOrAfter
explain: Both bind the statement to a login request that this browser session started, which stops an attacker injecting a response or ID token obtained elsewhere.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Conditional access: deciding at sign-in, and what happens after
question: Two Conditional Access policies apply to a sign-in: one requires MFA and one requires a compliant device. What does Entra require?
options: Either MFA or a compliant device
Both MFA and a compliant device
Only the newer policy
Only the stricter policy
explain: Microsoft's documentation: when multiple policies apply, all applicable policies must be satisfied, so the user needs MFA and a compliant device.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: The federation defender's checklist, and where to practise
question: During a suspected Golden SAML incident, which response step must come first?
options: Rotate the token-signing certificate
Regain administrative control of the IdP from clean machines and remove the attacker's access
Reset all user passwords
Disable SCIM
explain: Microsoft and CISA both stress that rotating keys while the attacker still controls the IdP only hands them the new key. Control first, then rotate twice, update relying parties and revoke tokens.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Access reviews and certification: asking again, and meaning it
question: A quarterly review of the admin console finishes 100% complete. One reviewer approved 212 of 212 items in about 2 seconds each. What should happen next?
options: Nothing: the campaign completed on time
Delete the reviewer's own account
Treat those decisions as unreviewed: re-run them with usage context or a different reviewer, and follow up with the reviewer
Approve all items automatically next quarter to save time
explain: Completion is not quality. Uniform approval at two seconds an item suggests nobody judged the need, so the decisions provide no assurance. Re-review with context, and treat reviewer behaviour as a metric.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: PAM vaults: check-out, rotation, and the Uber 2022 script
question: After the Uber pattern, a team moves the PAM admin password from a script into an environment variable on the same file server. What is still wrong?
options: Nothing: environment variables are encrypted
PowerShell cannot read environment variables
The password is now too short
A static PAM admin secret is still stored where people and processes on that server can read it, and the job still runs with vault admin rights
explain: Moving a static secret to another readable place does not satisfy IA-5(7)'s intent, and the job still holds far more privilege than reporting needs. Remove the secret and the excess privilege.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Service accounts and non-human identities
question: An engineer logs in interactively with the deployment service account because their own account lacks production rights. Which OWASP NHI risk is this, and why does it matter?
options: NHI10 Human Use of NHI: actions can no longer be tied to a person, and it bypasses the controls on the engineer's own account
NHI3 Vulnerable Third-Party NHI: the vendor is at fault
NHI6 Insecure Cloud Deployment Configurations: the cloud is misconfigured
It is not a risk if the password is strong
explain: Using a machine identity as a person breaks accountability and sidesteps the approval, MFA and review that apply to the engineer's own access.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
question: Applying Otsu to the difference of two aligned photos where nothing changed (only sensor noise), what do you expect?
options: An empty mask, because Otsu detects that there is only one class
An error from OpenCV
A mask flagging a sizable fraction of noise pixels
A mask with exactly one pixel
explain: Otsu has no notion of 'one class'. It maximizes between-class variance over all splits, which always exists, so it will cut the noise distribution somewhere near its middle. Guard against this with a minimum threshold or a test on the gap between class means.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: The IR lifecycle: NIST 800-61r3, CSF 2.0 and SANS PICERL
question: In the SANS PICERL model, why does containment include a "system back-up" step before long-term containment?
options: To restore the user's files faster
To take a forensic image of affected systems before they are wiped or rebuilt, preserving evidence
Because backups are required before any patch
To test the backup software
explain: The handbook places a forensic image (it names commercial forensic imaging tools such as FTK (Forensic Toolkit) and EnCase) before wiping and reimaging, so the evidence survives for prosecution or for the lessons-learned analysis.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence first: the order of volatility (RFC 3227)
question: RFC 3227 asks you to record the difference between the system clock and UTC. Why?
options: To meet a legal formatting rule
Because UTC is more secure
To detect whether the attacker changed the time zone
So that timestamps from this system can be aligned with other sources when building a timeline
explain: Timelines merge events from many machines. A server whose clock is 4 minutes fast puts its events in the wrong order relative to the firewall unless you record and correct the drift.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Linux artefacts: shell history, auth logs, cron, systemd, timestamps
question: A compromised server's /root/.bash_history has no commands from the intrusion window. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The attacker never used a root shell
Nothing: history is written at shell exit, can be disabled or redirected, and may never have been saved
The history file must have been edited
Root logins are not recorded by Linux
explain: Missing history is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. Look for other sources: auth logs, the journal, process accounting if enabled, file timestamps, and memory.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Ransomware response: pay or not, law enforcement and sanctions
question: During the 2017 NotPetya outbreak, a victim pays the ransom. What happens, according to Kaspersky's analysis?
options: They get a working key within hours
Nothing useful: the installation ID was random, so the attackers had no way to produce a key for that disk
Only the master boot record is restored
The payment is automatically refunded
explain: Kaspersky found the installation ID that a real ransomware operator needs for key recovery was generated from random data. NotPetya was a wiper presented as ransomware.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: When data becomes code: the one idea behind every injection
question: A program reads a city name and runs `eval("lookup('" + city + "')")`. A user types `Paris`. Another types `x') or delete_all('`. What does the second input do?
options: Nothing, because the city name is inside quotes
Python raises an error because quotes are not allowed in strings
It closes the quoted string early and adds a second function call to the expression
It only looks up a city literally named with those characters
explain: The built string becomes lookup('x') or delete_all(''). (Python's or runs delete_all only if lookup('x') returns a false value; an attacker would pick an operator that always runs the second call, but either way it is code the programmer never wrote.) The first quote in the input closes the string literal the programmer opened, so the rest is parsed as code. Quotes only protect data if the data cannot contain the closing quote.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Heartland and TalkTalk: SQL injection as the way in
question: The ICO found that TalkTalk's vulnerable pages came from Tiscali, which it had acquired years earlier. Which control most directly addresses that root cause?
options: A longer password policy for staff
Encrypting backups
An inventory of every web application you expose, including acquired ones, with owners who patch and test them
Moving the database to a different vendor
explain: The pages were vulnerable, unpatched and apparently unknown to the people responsible. Knowing what you run, and giving each system an owner, is the precondition for fixing it.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: MOVEit 2023: one SQL injection, thousands of victims
question: You patched MOVEit on 3 June 2023. What should you do next?
options: Nothing: the patch removes the vulnerability and any damage
Rotate the TLS certificate
Hunt for signs of earlier compromise, such as human2.aspx files, "Health Check Service" accounts and unusual requests in web logs
Switch the database engine
explain: Exploitation began on 27 May, before any patch existed. A web shell installed before patching keeps working afterwards, so you must look for persistence and data theft, then remove and report them.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Server-side template injection
question:
Which change fixes `render_template_string("

" + request.args["title"] + "

")` in a Flask (Python web framework) app?
options: Turn on autoescape
Strip the characters { and } from title

Use a constant template and pass title as a variable: render_template_string("

{{ title }}

", title=request.args["title"])
Use HTTPS
explain: The fix moves the input from template source to template data. Autoescape only affects output encoding, and stripping braces is a denylist that may miss other syntax such as {% %} or engine-specific forms.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Two shared rings: SQEs, CQEs, head and tail
question: A 4-entry SQ has tail counter 9. Which slot does the next SQE go into?
options: Slot 1, because 9 & 3 = 1
Slot 9, the tail value
Slot 0, because the ring is full after 4
Slot 2, because the next SQE goes one past the tail: 10 & 3 = 2
explain: The slot is `tail & (entries - 1)` = 9 & 3 = 1. The tail counter itself is never reset; it just keeps counting and the mask wraps it onto the 4 slots.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Inside a connected device: microcontrollers, flash and the boot ROM
question: Why are lock flags such as 'debugging disabled' stored in OTP bits rather than in flash?
options: An OTP bit, once set, cannot be cleared by software that later gains control
OTP is faster to read at boot
Flash cannot store single bits
OTP is encrypted automatically
explain: The point of a lock is that nobody can undo it later, including malicious code. OTP bits only change one way. A flag in flash could be rewritten by anyone who can write flash. Speed and encryption are not the reason.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Secure boot: a chain of trust that starts in ROM
question: A bootloader computes SHA-256 of the application and compares it with a hash stored next to the application in flash. What does this protect against?
options: An attacker who can write flash replacing the application
Accidental corruption of the application, but not deliberate replacement
Both corruption and replacement
Neither
explain: Whoever can write the new application can also write its new hash, so a bare hash only detects accidents. A signature checked against a key fingerprint the attacker cannot change (in OTP) is what stops deliberate replacement.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: A/B slots, trial boots and recovery from a bad update
question: A camera is on trial with firmware 4.0 (PENDING_VERIFY) when the power fails. What does ESP-IDF's bootloader do on the next start, with rollback enabled?
options: Boots 4.0 again and waits for confirmation
Erases both slots
Boots the factory image and burns the anti-rollback fuse
Marks 4.0 ABORTED and boots the previous valid image
explain: An image that reboots while still PENDING_VERIFY was never confirmed. ESP-IDF marks it aborted and returns to the last valid application. Nothing is erased, and the security version is only raised after a successful confirmation.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Device vulnerability handling: disclosure, SBOMs and the CRA
question: Under the CRA, which deadline applies to a manufacturer's first notification of an actively exploited vulnerability?
options: 24 hours for an early warning
72 hours
14 days
One month
explain: The early warning is due within 24 hours, the main notification within 72 hours, and the final report no later than 14 days after a fix or mitigation is available. One month is the final-report deadline for severe incidents.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototype pollution: one request changes every object
question: A code reviewer sees `target[k1][k2] = v` where `k1` and `k2` come from a JSON body. The team proposes rejecting only the key `__proto__`. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: __proto__ is the only way to reach Object.prototype
k1 = constructor and a deeper write via prototype still reach Object.prototype; refuse all three names or use own-key checks and null-prototype objects
JSON.parse already removes __proto__, so the check is redundant
The check must be case-insensitive because JavaScript property names ignore case
explain: MDN describes the constructor.prototype route explicitly, and our test showed it working even with --disable-proto=delete. JSON.parse keeps __proto__ as an own key rather than removing it, and property names are case-sensitive.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: ReDoS: a regular expression that blocks every user
question: Why is a 2-second regex match worse on a Node.js server than on a server that runs each request on its own thread?
options: Because V8 cannot run regular expressions on a worker thread
Because Node.js restarts the process whenever a regex exceeds one second
It is not worse: Node.js automatically moves regexes to the Worker Pool
Because Node.js runs every request's JavaScript on one Event Loop, so the match delays all other clients, not just the attacker
explain: Regex matching is ordinary JavaScript work on the Event Loop. The Worker Pool runs only specific I/O and CPU APIs. A thread-per-request server would lose one thread; a Node.js process loses all its JavaScript capacity for the duration.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Deserialisation in JavaScript: node-serialize to React2Shell
question: A team wants to send a 'job' object containing a callback function from one service to another and proposes node-serialize. What should they do instead?
options: Use node-serialize but strip the function marker with a regex
Use eval on the receiving side but inside a try/catch
Base64-encode the serialised object so it cannot be tampered with
Send only data (for example a job type name and JSON parameters), validate it with a schema, and map the type name to code the receiving service already contains
explain: Code should never travel as data across a trust boundary. An allowlist of job types mapped to local functions gives the same flexibility with no deserialisation of code. Regex stripping is a blocklist, try/catch does not stop code from running, and Base64 is an encoding, not protection.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Electron: when XSS in a desktop app becomes code execution
question: Which single change would have broken the Discord chain at the navigation step?
options: Raising the bug bounty
Turning nodeIntegration on
Adding the sandbox attribute to the embed iframes, so they cannot navigate the top-level window
Loading the embed over HTTP instead of HTTPS
explain: Both Discord's interim fix and Electron's advisory workaround were to sandbox iframes. Without the top-level navigation, the iframe's XSS stays inside the iframe, which has no access to the main window's built-ins or preload API.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: mimalloc: three free lists per page
question: A loop does `p = malloc(48); free(p);` a billion times on one thread. Without `local_free` (frees pushed straight onto `free`), what would mimalloc lose?
options: The guarantee that the slow path runs regularly, so remote frees and deferred work could wait forever
Correctness: blocks would be handed out twice
Locality, because blocks would come from other pages
Nothing; local_free exists only for debugging
explain: With one list, the same block is pushed and popped forever and free never empties, so malloc_generic never runs. thread_free would never be collected and deferred-free callbacks would never fire. local_free makes free run dry after a bounded number of allocations.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
question: A test with 5 client processes runs for 10 minutes and 40 writes end as info. Roughly how many operations can be concurrent near the end of the history?
options: At most 5, because there are only 5 processes
Exactly 40, the info writes alone
Zero, because the test is over
Up to about 45: the 5 live processes plus 40 writes that might still take effect
explain: Each info write stays open until the end of the history, and the crashed processes were replaced by fresh ones that keep issuing operations. So concurrency near the end is the live processes plus every unresolved info op, which is what makes checking expensive.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: The knobs, and how fast the space grows
question: You add one more knob to the matmul kernel: a vector width with 3 legal values. Everything else is unchanged. What happens to the 6000-configuration space?
options: It grows by 3 configurations, to 6003
It triples, to 18000 configurations
It stays at 6000 because vector width is derived from BLOCK_K
It grows only if you also add shapes to the key
explain: Knobs combine multiplicatively: every existing configuration is now three configurations, one per vector width. This is why autotuning is a search problem rather than a loop over a list, and why pruning matters before you compile anything.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
question: Why do people benchmark packet I/O with 64 byte frames rather than 1500 byte frames?
options: Because they maximize packets per second, so fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, syscalls, metadata) dominate and are exposed
Because 64 byte frames are the most common size on real networks
Because NICs can only DMA 64 bytes at a time
Because larger frames do not fit in a 2 KiB packet buffer
explain: Throughput in bits is the same, but small frames mean the most packets per second, and most driver and stack costs are per packet, not per byte. That is the worst case a data plane must survive.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
question: With SPDK's deferred-doorbell option on, a thread calls spdk_nvme_ns_cmd_read 16 times and then calls spdk_nvme_qpair_process_completions once. How many SQ tail doorbell writes did those 16 submissions need?
options: 0, NVMe needs no doorbell
explain: With the option set, submission only builds commands in the SQ ring; the doorbell is rung inside the poll call, once for everything submitted since the last poll.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Driver signing: from cross-signing to Microsoft's portal
question: A vendor wants a new kernel driver to reach retail users through Windows Update on Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025. Which signing route fits?
options: HLK testing and WHCP (dashboard) signing
Attestation signing with an EV certificate
Cross-signing with a commercial CA certificate
Test signing with the TESTSIGNING boot option
explain: Attestation-signed drivers cannot be published to Windows Update for retail audiences and do not load on Windows Server 2016 and later. Cross-signing is no longer accepted, and test signing is for development machines. HLK-tested WHCP signing covers client and Server.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Buffers, double fetches and Microsoft's driver security checklist
question: Which checklist item most directly reduces the chance that an overclocking utility's driver becomes a BYOVD tool on PCs from other manufacturers?
options: Restrict software-only drivers to the hardware they serve, for example by checking SMBIOS before enabling capabilities
Add SAL annotations
Use NonPagedPoolNx for allocations
Run BinSkim before release
explain: Software-only drivers can be loaded on any PC, which is what makes them portable attack tools. Microsoft's checklist says they must verify they run on the intended hardware, using a unique PnP (Plug and Play) ID or an SMBIOS check. The other items improve quality but do not limit where the driver works.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: App Control driver policies: allow what you run, deny what you know
question: Your allowlist trusts Fabrikam drivers at WHQLPublisher level. Microsoft's blocklist, deployed as a second policy, denies Fabrikam toyfan.sys up to 1.4. Will ToyFan 1.3 load?
options: No, because a file must pass every active policy and explicit deny rules are processed first
Yes, because the allow rule names the publisher
Yes, because the blocklist contains Allow All rules
It depends on the order the policies were deployed
explain: With multiple policies, a file must be allowed by each of them. The blocklist policy denies ToyFan 1.3; its Allow All rules only mean it does not restrict anything else. Within any one policy, explicit deny rules take precedence over allow rules.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Responding to a BYOVD alert, and the cost of kernel code
question: After removing a malicious driver's service and file, and updating the blocklist, why is a reboot part of eradication?
options: To rotate the BitLocker key
Because a driver that is already loaded stays in kernel memory until restart; removing the file and adding blocks does not unload it
Because Sysmon only logs after a reboot
Because the blocklist only works in Safe Mode
explain: Microsoft's blocklist page notes that already running drivers the policy would block keep running until the computer restarts. Deleting the file does not unmap the code from kernel memory either.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
question: In the PyTorch 2 ablation, disabling both fusion and inlining made compiled models slower than eager. Why?
options: torch.compile adds Python overhead per op
Inductor decomposes large operators into many primitives and relies on fusion to recombine them
Triton kernels are slower than CUDA kernels
Graph breaks increase without fusion
explain: The paper explains that decompositions break large optimized operators into smaller primitive ops, and fusion recombines them. Without fusion and inlining each primitive becomes its own kernel with its own HBM round trip, so the result is slower than eager's hand-written kernels.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
question: Your transfer set is 2 million unlabeled product photos plus 5,000 labeled ones. What is a sensible way to set alpha?
options: alpha = 0, since human labels are more reliable than any teacher
alpha = 0.5 everywhere, so neither term dominates
Copy the PyTorch tutorial's 0.25 soft and 0.75 hard weights
alpha = 1 (pure distillation) on the unlabeled photos, and tune alpha jointly with T on held-out data for the labeled ones
explain: Unlabeled examples have no hard-label term, so only the soft loss applies to them. Where labels exist, the right mix is an empirical question: Hinton et al. found a low hard-label weight best, the tutorial uses the opposite, and T shifts the balance, so tune T and alpha together on held-out data.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: An LLM distillation pipeline: logits, tokenizers, traces, compute
question: You stored each position's top-64 teacher entries and renormalized them to sum to 1. Compared with full-distribution distillation, what should you expect, and what is the cheapest mitigation Busbridge et al. found?
options: A student that is too confident on the kept tokens; mix in cross-entropy on the real next tokens
A student that is too uncertain; raise the temperature
No effect, since the dropped tokens carry almost no probability
A student whose vocabulary shrinks to 64 tokens; store the full distribution instead
explain: Renormalizing assigns zero to every token outside the top k, so the target is sharper than the teacher and even a perfect copy of the teacher is penalized (0.223 nats in the toy). In their study top-128 cost 0.11 nats, and a 0.7 distillation plus 0.3 next-token mix recovered it to within 0.01 nats.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
question: In GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, what does each KV head serve?
options: A group of 4 query heads
One query head; the other 24 are unused
All 32 query heads
8 consecutive tokens
explain: Query heads are split into 8 groups of 4, and each group shares one key head and one value head.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
question: Which statement about H2O is correct?
options: It needs the model to be fine-tuned
It scores tokens by attention they received in past steps, as a proxy for future importance
It keeps every token but at lower precision
It keeps only heavy hitters and no recent tokens
explain: H2O is training-free and uses local statistics: the sum of attention each token received so far. The paper finds this as effective as using future attention, and that keeping both heavy hitters and recent tokens is needed.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Build and test it: quantize real keys, then evict on a needle test
question: You deploy SnapKV for a RAG service and accuracy is poor on facts buried in the documents. Your harness shows that compression runs before the user's question is appended, with a 64-token observation window. What is the most direct fix?
options: Switch to StreamingLLM
Lower compression_ratio to 0.1 and keep the 64-token window
Compress after the question is in the prompt, with an observation window about the question's length
Quantize the cache to FP8 instead
explain: In the lab's run (50 trials per setting), SnapKV without the question scored 0% at every ratio, and a 64-query window diluted by filler reached at most 28%; a 16-query window over the question reached 98% to 100% even at 75% removed. StreamingLLM drops old documents by position, and FP8 does not reduce the token count.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
question: A request's blocks are h0 to h9. HBM holds h0 to h3. The CPU tier holds h0 to h6 and h8, h9. What gets loaded from CPU, and what is recomputed?
options: Load h4 to h6 and h8, h9; recompute h7
Load h4 to h6; recompute h7, h8, h9
Load nothing; recompute h4 to h9, since the CPU tier has a gap
Load h0 to h6 again from CPU to refresh them; recompute h7 to h9
explain: The usable prefix stops at the first block that is nowhere: h7. h4 to h6 extend the GPU hit contiguously, so they are loaded. h8 and h9 were computed after a context that includes h7, which must be recomputed, so they are recomputed along with it.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Hands-on: configure an offload tier and measure it
question: A GPU holds 40 GB of KV cache. You enable vLLM's OffloadingConnector with `cpu_bytes_to_use` set to 30 GB. How many extra hits should the CPU tier add?
options: About 75% more, since 30 GB is 75% of HBM
Twice as many, since the cache doubles in size
It depends only on the eviction policy
Almost none: blocks are copied out as soon as they are computed, so a tier smaller than HBM only mirrors blocks HBM still holds
explain: Offloading is immediate, so the CPU tier holds copies of recent blocks, most of which are still in HBM. Only a tier larger than the aggregate GPU KV cache keeps blocks HBM has already evicted. vLLM's tuning guide says exactly this.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
question: A node at (10, 3) receives a message stamped (8, 7) when its physical clock reads 9. What is the result?
explain: l = max(10, 8, 9) = 10 equals only the old l, so c = 3 + 1 = 4, giving (10, 4). The message's counter 7 is ignored because its l is smaller: (8, 7) is already less than (10, 3). Taking max(c, cm) + 1 here would be a bug that inflates c.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Inside the encoders: markers, [MASK] padding and training
question: ColBERTv2 distills a cross-encoder with a KL-divergence loss over a 64-way score distribution instead of regressing the cross-encoder's raw scores with mean squared error. What is the reason the paper gives?
options: KL divergence is cheaper to compute than MSE
ColBERT's scores (sums of cosines) have a restricted scale that may not line up with the cross-encoder's output scale; KL compares the distributions over passages instead
MSE cannot be backpropagated through a max operation
The cross-encoder only outputs binary labels
explain: A sum of 32 cosines lives in a fixed range, while a cross-encoder's logits can be on any scale. Matching softmax distributions over the same 64 passages only asks ColBERT to rank them the same way, which is what retrieval needs.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
question: Why does writing reasoning tokens let a fixed-depth transformer solve problems it cannot solve in one pass?
options: Generated tokens are fed back as inputs, so later passes can build on earlier results, increasing effective serial depth
Longer outputs give the attention softmax a sharper distribution
Each written token adds new trainable parameters at inference
The KV cache stores the answer before it is written
explain: Each pass has bounded depth L. Feeding outputs back chains passes together, so n written steps allow roughly n x L layers of sequential computation. Coconut keeps this feedback loop but passes a vector instead of a token.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why superposition works: continuous thoughts and graph reachability
question: In the 7-node example, why does G never appear in any thought?
options: Its weight is filtered out by the MLP for being too small
No edge leads into G, so it is not reachable; the edge G to D is only attended when G is already in the set
G is a candidate, and candidates are excluded from thoughts
G appears in t3 but is cancelled by layer normalization
explain: Layer 2 attends to edges by their source. G's only edge leaves G, and G is never reachable from A, so that edge never matches and nothing adds G. The final measurement then reads 0 for G and 0.408 for F.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
question: A B-tree with pages of 128 keys and a model with min_err = -40, max_err = +60 both index the same array. In terms of the final search, which statement is right?
options: The model is worse because its errors can be negative
Both leave a range of about 100 to 128 slots to search; they are the same kind of object
The B-tree is exact and the model is approximate, so only the model needs a final search
The model needs no final search if its average error is small
explain: A page is a position estimate with min error 0 and max error 127. The model's range is 101 slots. Both end with a bounded search. That equivalence is the core observation of the paper: a B-tree already is a model with error bounds.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
question: In Bigtable's design a weak model makes some blocks much larger than the target size tau. What breaks?
options: Lookups return wrong rows
Range scans stop working because the model is not monotonic
Nothing is incorrect; block sizes just become uneven, which can cost some read efficiency
Every lookup must now search neighbouring blocks
explain: Records are assigned to block floor(f(k) / tau) by the model itself, so the predicted block is correct by construction. A monotonic f keeps keys sorted so scans still work. A poor fit only makes block sizes less uniform.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Training: ranking loss plus the FLOPs regularizer
question: After raising lambda_q a lot, MS MARCO MRR@10 drops slightly but queries are much faster. What most likely changed?
options: Document vectors got denser
The vocabulary shrank
The ranking loss switched to L1
Query vectors have fewer non-zeros, so fewer posting lists are traversed
explain: lambda_q only penalizes the query representation. Fewer query terms means fewer posting lists to read, at some cost in matching power.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaRank: weight each pair by what a swap does to NDCG
question: After computing lambdas for a query, a teammate finds the per-document pushes sum to 0.37. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing: sums vary from query to query
The query has more relevant than irrelevant documents
The learning rate is too high
There is a bug: each pair adds equal and opposite pushes, so the total must be 0
explain: Every pair adds lambda to one document and subtracts it from the other, so the sum over a query is exactly zero (up to rounding).

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
question: In the toy, why did $k_A$ and $k_B$ read back perfectly after the first two writes?
options: Because they were written first
Because the values 4 and 2 are small
Because the keys are unit length and orthogonal, so $k_A^\top k_B = 0$ and nothing leaks
Because S was reset between writes
explain: Reading $Sk_A = 4(k_A^\top k_A) + 2(k_B^\top k_A) = 4\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 0 = 4$. Orthonormal keys make the memory exact; overlap is what causes interference.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: One family, many transitions: RetNet to GLA, Mamba2, RWKV-7, KDA
question: A head keeps a variable's value in key channel 3 and the current topic in key channel 7. The next token should drop the variable but keep the topic, and its own write is needed for something else. Which transition can do this?
options: Mamba2's scalar $\alpha_tI$
RetNet's fixed $\gamma I$
A per-channel $\text{Diag}(\alpha_t)$, as in GLA or KDA
DeltaNet's $I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$ alone
explain: Only a diagonal gate can scale channel 3 toward 0 while leaving channel 7 near 1. Scalar gates shrink both equally. The delta rule could erase channel 3, but only by spending this token's single write on it.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Users, groups and root: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
question: Why is /etc/passwd readable by every user while /etc/shadow is readable only by root?
options: Programs everywhere need to map UIDs to names, but password hashes can be guessed offline if copied
Because /etc/passwd is encrypted and /etc/shadow is not
It is a historical accident with no security effect
So that users can change other users' passwords
explain: Name and UID lookups happen constantly, so passwd must be public. A copied hash can be attacked with unlimited offline guesses, so hashes were moved to shadow, which is unreadable to ordinary users.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Processes, PIDs, process trees and signals
question: Which observation is the strongest sign of compromise on a web server?
options: sshd running as root with PPID 1
bash running as www-data whose parent is an apache2 worker
A process named kworker
cron running as root
explain: sshd under PID 1 and cron as root are normal. Kernel threads are named kworker but have no executable. A shell spawned by a web server worker is the classic sign of command injection (untrusted input ending up in a shell command) or a Shellshock-style bug.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: regreSSHion: a signal handler race in the SSH server
question: Why was LoginGraceTime 0 an effective emergency mitigation for regreSSHion?
options: With no login time limit, the SIGALRM handler never fires, so there is no race to win
It disables password login
