options: Never: error keeps falling as a power law in T
Once T exceeds roughly k to the power beta, where k is the effective tail cut; after that error plateaus at the missing tail mass
Immediately: synthetic data never helps
Only when the teacher's perplexity exceeds the student's
explain: Data from a tail-cut generator only teaches the head of the distribution. Once the student has learned the head, the remaining error is the mass of the items it never sees, and more samples from the same generator cannot reveal them.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
question: A lab wants its 2027 pretraining mix to stay anchored to human text. Which plan does this lesson support best?
options: Keep pre-LLM snapshots and other known-human sources permanently in the mix, and treat classifier or watermark filtering of new crawls as an extra layer
Rely on an AI-text classifier to remove all model-written pages from new crawls, then drop the old snapshots to save space
Rely on watermarks, since every model that writes web text embeds one
Ignore provenance, since accumulating any data at all prevents every form of collapse
explain: Detectors can be evaded by paraphrasing and are bounded by how close AI text is to human text, and watermarks cover only cooperating generators. Known-human data kept permanently is the anchor that does not depend on detection. Accumulation bounds error but does not by itself protect the tails.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
question: The 10,000-byte file is mapped writable with MAP_SHARED and length 12,288. You write p[10500] = 'x'. What happens?
options: SIGBUS, because byte 10,500 is past end of file
The file grows to 10,501 bytes
The write succeeds in memory but is never written to the file
SIGSEGV, because shared mappings cannot be written past EOF
explain: Byte 10,500 is in page 2, the last partial page, so it is mapped and zero-filled. mmap(2) says modifications to that tail region are not written out to the file. mmap never changes a file's size; use ftruncate first if you need the file to grow. SIGBUS would only come from touching page 3, which is wholly beyond EOF.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
question: strace -c on a busy program shows 2 million read calls taking 4 s of system time. Without strace, the program's total run time is 1.5 s. What is the best reading?
options: The program spends 4 s in read; strace measures it exactly
strace double-counts calls made by threads
read must be served by the vDSO in the untraced run
The call count is trustworthy, but strace's own overhead inflates the times, so measure time without it
explain: Tracing stops the program around every call, so times under strace are inflated; strace(1) warns that a traced process runs more slowly. The count of 2 million is what the program really does, and it suggests a bigger buffer. read has no vDSO version.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
question: Your team wants a fleet-wide p99 dashboard. Each of 40 hosts exports its own p99 every minute. What should you do?
options: Average the 40 p99 values, weighting by request count
Take the maximum of the 40 p99 values, which is exactly the fleet p99
Export histogram bucket counts from each host, sum them, and compute p99 from the merged histogram
Take the median of the 40 p99 values to ignore outlier hosts
explain: Percentiles are not additive; neither the weighted mean nor the max of per-host p99s equals the fleet p99 in general. Summed histogram counts describe the combined distribution, so the percentile computed from them is right up to bucket resolution.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Signalling firewalls: message categories, home routing, monitoring
question: A message type that only the subscriber's home network should send about that subscriber arrives from a network that does not own the IMSI. Which category rule catches it?
options: Category 1: block the message type everywhere
Category 3: check trajectory plausibility
None: home routing handles it
Category 2: check the sender against the IMSI's home network
explain: That is the definition of category 2: legitimate between operators, but only from the subscriber's home. Blocking the type everywhere would break roaming, and trajectory checks apply to messages from the visited network.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: 5G identity privacy: SUPI, SUCI and ECIES concealment
question: Why do two SUCIs for the same subscriber, generated a second apart, look completely different?
options: The MSIN changes every second
The home network rotates its private key every second
The phone adds a timestamp to the MSIN
Each SUCI uses a fresh ephemeral key pair, so the shared secret, keys and ciphertext all change
explain: ECIES generates a new ephemeral key pair per encryption. That gives unlinkability: a passive listener cannot tell that two SUCIs belong to the same person.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Lawful interception: a built-in wiretap, and the Athens affair
question: Which audit design would most reliably find an Athens-style tap?
options: Reviewing the list of warrants in the LI management system
Checking that every warrant has been provisioned
Asking engineers whether they set up any taps
Querying each switch for its active intercepts and comparing them with the warrant master list, using logs the switch software cannot alter
explain: The rogue taps existed only in the switches, so a review that starts from the management system sees nothing. The authors recommend comparing what the exchange actually monitors with the active warrants, with logging rogue software cannot modify.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: GNSS: how a receiver finds position and time, and what jamming does
question: According to EASA, why is spoofing considered a bigger safety risk to aircraft than jamming?
options: Spoofing equipment is always more powerful
Spoofing only affects military aircraft
Jamming effects are usually immediate and noticeable, while spoofing may be harder to detect and not immediate
Jamming is legal
explain: EASA SIB 2022-02R4: jamming typically produces immediate, recognisable failures; detection of spoofing may be more difficult and not immediate, thus posing more safety risk.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
question: In the sweep, `merged[-1][1]` is the end of the last merged block. A developer writes `merged[-1][1] = e` instead of `max(merged[-1][1], e)`. On the toy resume (generous convention), what total does the code report?
options: 132 months, the bug never triggers
180 months, it stops merging
129 months: B, nested inside A, cuts A's block short by 3 months
137 months, gaps are counted
explain: When B (ending Dec 2017) is merged into A's block, the end is overwritten from Mar 2018 to Dec 2017, losing Jan to Mar 2018. C still starts a new block, D and E extend it correctly, so the total is 31 + 98 = 129. Nested intervals are exactly the case max() exists for.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
question: A model has pass@1 = 0.01 on a problem. Roughly how many independent samples give a 63% chance of at least one correct answer?
options: About 10
About 63
About 100
About 1,000
explain: $1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.634$. In general, $k \approx 1/p$ samples give about $1 - 1/e = 63\%$ coverage for small $p$.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
question: A product mostly receives easy prompts that the model already solves 70% of the time. Which allocation does the paper's evidence favor?
options: Deep lookahead search against a PRM
Spend the budget sequentially (revise or keep reasoning) rather than on aggressive PRM search
Skip any verifier and return the first sample
Always use the maximum number of parallel samples
explain: On easy bins, sequential revisions did best and beam search degraded with budget. Light selection (vote or weighted best-of-N) over a revision chain is the safer choice.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
question: During inference with a TTT model, what changes as the model reads a long prompt?
options: Nothing; all weights are frozen at inference
Only the inner weights W inside each TTT layer, which act as a per-sequence hidden state
All model parameters, via backpropagation of next-token loss on the prompt
The projections theta_K, theta_V and theta_Q, which adapt to the prompt
explain: The inner loop runs at inference, so each layer's W takes gradient steps on its self-supervised loss. The outer parameters (projections, W_0, the rest of the network) are learned in training and frozen. No next-token loss is backpropagated at inference.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
question: Which change would you expect to hurt the Titans neural memory most, according to the paper's ablation?
options: Removing the persistent memory tokens
Removing the 1D convolutions after the projections
Removing weight decay (the forget mechanism)
Replacing SiLU with GELU in the projections
explain: Table 5: without weight decay perplexity rises from 27.01 to 29.04, the largest drop, with momentum next (28.98). Persistent memory matters least (27.63). The activation swap was not tested, so the paper gives no evidence for it. SiLU multiplies x by sigmoid of x, a smooth ReLU-like curve much like GELU.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: After Titans: better objectives, optimal solvers, and replication
question: A memory keeps getting corrupted by rare tokens with huge values (say, a burst of numbers in a table). Which Miras variant targets this directly?
options: Moneta, because the l3 loss grows faster for large errors
Memora, because KL retention keeps weights on a simplex
Yaad, because the Huber loss caps how far one large error can move the memory
None; only a forget gate can help
explain: Huber is squared error for small errors and absolute error beyond delta_t, so the step size stops growing with the error and one outlier cannot drag the memory all the way to its value. An l3 loss does the opposite, weighting large errors even more, and KL retention is about how weights are kept and forgotten, not about outliers.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay
question: Why are full magazines only ever created as a side effect of frees, never allocated directly on the alloc path?
options: Allocating a full magazine needs M objects, which would mean M slab-layer trips, and for the magazine cache itself it would recurse forever
Full magazines are larger than empty ones
The depot lock forbids allocation
Frees are rarer than allocs
explain: Allocating empty magazines on the free path is cheap and safe. Pre-filling a magazine on the alloc path would need many objects at once, and since magazines are themselves allocated from an object cache, the first magazine allocation would need a magazine: infinite recursion. The paper notes this explicitly.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: PEAK and TaHiTI: from backlog to handover
question: A TaHiTI hunt needs 60 days of process creation events with command lines, but the domain controllers only record process creation without command lines. What is the outcome?
options: Proven: missing data means the attacker deleted it
Failed: the required data is not available, which is itself a finding
Inconclusive: run the same queries again next week
Disproven: nothing malicious was found
explain: TaHiTI says that when 'the required data may simply not be available', the hunt can be considered failed, and that 'can still lead to valuable lessons learned'. Here the lesson is a logging recommendation: enable command-line capture (event 4688 with command lines, or Sysmon) on domain controllers. Calling it disproven would claim a check that never happened.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in EDR data II: LSASS, WMI and sensors that go quiet
question: In the HSE timeline, antivirus detected Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on 31 March in monitor mode. Which recurring hunt would most directly have surfaced it?
options: Stacking the DNS names every workstation resolves
A weekly review of all security-control detections, grouped by threat name and device, including ones not blocked
Baselining VPN logins
Searching for the ransomware's file hash
explain: The evidence was a detection already recorded by a security control. Grouping all such detections by tool name and device, and treating 'not blocked' or 'remediated' as still needing a look, puts two well-known attack tools on one workstation at the top of the list. The ransomware hash did not exist on that machine until 14 May.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: From hunt to detection: the FireEye countermeasures
question: A hunt for Office applications starting shells found one real intrusion and three benign matches over four weeks. When it becomes a detection, what should those four events become?
options: Allowlist entries for all four
A threat intelligence report
Test cases: the intrusion as must-match, the three benign matches as must-not-match
Nothing; they are history
explain: The hunt has produced labelled examples, which is precisely what a detection's unit tests need. The real event proves the rule still fires after future changes; the benign ones measure and guard against false positives. Allowlisting the true positive would hide the very thing the rule exists to catch.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Strategic, operational, tactical and technical intelligence
question: Which product is *operational* intelligence in the MWR and NCSC sense that FIRST summarises?
options: A warning to the CISO that a group hitting two sector peers this week uses the same VPN model you run
A list of 2,000 malicious domains for the web proxy
A ten-year forecast of state-sponsored espionage trends for the board
A YARA rule for a malware family
explain: Operational intelligence is specific to the organisation and warns defenders of an impending attack. The domain list and the YARA rule are technical (or tactical, depending on convention), and the ten-year forecast is strategic.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The Diamond Model: one event, four corners
question: Your endpoint detection tool found malware on one laptop and you have the C2 domain from reversing it. Which pivot is most likely to find other compromised machines in your own network?
options: Search DNS and proxy logs for other hosts that resolved or contacted the C2 domain and its IPs
Look up the adversary's motive
Check the malware's capacity against CVE lists
Wait for the attacker's next phishing email
explain: That is the infrastructure-to-victim pivot (pivot 4 in the paper's example): hosts talking to the same C2 infrastructure are candidate victims. It uses data you already hold, which is why victim-centred work starts there.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Analytic tradecraft: bias and competing hypotheses
question: Why did Kaspersky treat the identical Rich header with suspicion rather than as proof?
options: The header's contents contradicted the binary it was attached to, and a 100% match with a famous group seemed too convenient
Rich headers are encrypted and cannot be read
Lazarus never uses Windows
TLP:RED forbade attribution
explain: The header described a Visual Studio 6 build while the code could only come from Visual Studio 2010's runtime, so it had been copied in. Combined with other inconsistencies, the 'perfect' match pointed to a false flag.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: What a threat model is: four questions before the code
question: A product manager asks: 'Is our app secure?' What is the threat modeler's best first reply?
options: Secure against whom, protecting what, and for how long?
Yes, because we use HTTPS and hashed passwords
No system is secure, so the question is meaningless
Run a vulnerability scanner and report the score
explain: Security is relative to an adversary and an asset. Listing controls (HTTPS) answers question 3 before questions 1 and 2. A scanner finds some implementation bugs but says nothing about design threats.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: STRIDE per element: from a diagram to a threat list
question: Why does STRIDE per element NOT list spoofing for a data store?
options: Data stores are always encrypted
Spoofing applies to things that have an identity to fake, like users and processes; a store's threats are its data being changed, read, or made unavailable
Data stores sit inside the trust boundary
Spoofing is the same as tampering
explain: The table records where threats cluster in practice. Stores are not always encrypted or internal, and spoofing differs from tampering: one fakes an identity, the other changes data.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles II: least privilege, two keys and shared parts
question: A payment system lets one clerk both create a new supplier and approve payments to it. Which principle is missing?
options: Least common mechanism
Separation of privilege: creating a payee and approving payment should need two different people
Fail-safe defaults
Work factor
explain: With both powers in one pair of hands, a single dishonest or deceived person can pay themselves. Two keys held by different people means no single breach of trust is enough.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers
question: A service has 200 GB allocated, of which 40 GB is touched every few seconds and the rest is idle for minutes. Which configuration best fits tiered memory?
options: 64 GB DRAM and 160 GB CXL, with the OS demoting idle pages to CXL
160 GB DRAM and 40 GB CXL, so hot pages are guaranteed to fit
200 GB of CXL only, since CXL is cheaper per GB
64 GB DRAM and 160 GB of SSD swap, since swap is cheapest
explain: The hot 40 GB fits in 64 GB of DRAM with headroom, and idle pages go to cheaper CXL where they remain directly addressable. All-CXL puts hot data 2x farther away, and swap-only makes every access to a cold page a fault plus an SSD read.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
question: Why does TPP not use CXL memory as a fast swap device instead of a NUMA node?
options: Swap cannot be placed on byte-addressable memory
CXL devices do not support writes
Swap semantics turn every access into a major fault and a full-page copy, losing CXL's direct cache-line loads
The kernel cannot migrate pages to CXL
explain: The value of CXL is that warm pages can be read in place with a load at roughly 2x DRAM latency. Treating it as swap would add a fault and a 4 KiB copy to every access to a swapped page.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
question: A user connects over HTTPS to a phishing site, `paypa1-login.example`, which has a valid certificate for that exact name. Which TLS promise failed?
options: None: TLS authenticated paypa1-login.example correctly; deciding it is the wrong site is outside TLS
Authentication, because the certificate is fake
Confidentiality, because the attacker can read the traffic
Integrity, because the page content was changed
explain: TLS binds the connection to the name the client asked for. The certificate is genuine for that name. Look-alike domains are a human and policy problem (and a reason CT monitoring exists), not a protocol failure.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: TLS 1.2, RSA key exchange and forward secrecy
question: A bank's server used TLS 1.2 with `TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256` for five years. Its private key leaks today. What can an attacker who recorded traffic for those five years do?
options: Decrypt the recorded sessions, because each premaster secret was encrypted to that key
Nothing, because AES-GCM is still secure
Only impersonate the bank from now on
Decrypt only sessions from the last 24 hours
explain: TLS_RSA_ suites use RSA key exchange: the premaster secret of every session was RSA-encrypted to the leaked key. AES-GCM being strong does not help when the key that protects its keys is gone.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Hostname checks and the code that turns verification off
question: A developer gets `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` talking to `https://billing.internal`, whose certificate comes from the company's private CA. What is the right fix?
options: Set verify=False for that one call
Set check_hostname=False but keep CERT_REQUIRED
Load the company root CA into the client's trust settings (for example cafile=...) and keep both checks on
Switch to plain HTTP inside the network
explain: The error is correct: the client does not know the private CA. Teaching it that CA keeps full authentication. Disabling either check lets any machine on the path impersonate billing.internal.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Revocation: CRL, OCSP, stapling, and why short-lived certs won
question: Why do browsers treat a failed OCSP lookup as "good" (soft-fail) rather than rejecting the site?
options: Because hard-fail would break sites on every flaky network or captive portal and turn OCSP responders into single points of failure
Because OCSP responses are never signed
Because revocation was abolished by the CA/B Forum
Because OCSP only works for EV certificates
explain: Availability forced soft-fail. The unfortunate consequence is that the attacker who matters, one on your network path, can block the lookup and get the soft-fail outcome.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: goto fail: one duplicated line that skipped the signature check
question: Why did certificate pinning not protect against goto fail?
options: Pins were stored in the wrong format
Pinning only works on Android
goto fail disabled pinning
The attacker presented the site's genuine certificate chain, which matched any pin; the broken part was the check that the handshake was signed by that certificate's key
explain: Pinning checks which keys appear in the chain. goto fail let the attacker show the real chain while proving nothing about possessing its key.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
question: A softmax kernel computes the row sum with tl.sum on a block loaded with mask=col < n_cols and no other= argument. What is the most likely symptom?
options: A compile error, because masks require other=
Correct results, because masked lanes are always zero
Results that are wrong or NaN only when n_cols is not a power of two
Results that are wrong for every input
explain: Without other= the masked lanes are undefined, and tl.sum adds them in. When n_cols is a power of two, BLOCK_SIZE equals n_cols and there are no masked lanes, so the bug hides in tests that use round sizes.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Everything is a token: Chameleon and Emu3
question: Chameleon-7B diverged without QK-Norm, and an ablation without image generation did not diverge. Which explanation does the paper give?
options: Sharing all weights across modalities of different entropy lets norms grow, and softmax's shift invariance means the loss does not resist it
Image tokens have a larger vocabulary than text tokens
The VQ decoder sends exploding gradients back into the transformer
Images are longer than text, so the learning rate is too high
explain: Softmax(z) = softmax(z + c), so a uniform growth in logits costs nothing in cross-entropy, and with modalities competing the norms creep up until bf16 overflows. QK-Norm and z-loss add the missing resistance. The tokenizer is frozen, so it sends no gradients.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
question: A team runs exactly one Redis process per VM on a multi-tenant cloud. Which protection does the guest kernel's user/kernel split still provide that the hypervisor does not?
options: It stops other tenants from reading Redis's memory
It is required for the VM to reach the network card
It protects the guest kernel's code and data from a bug or exploit in Redis, inside that one VM
It prevents Redis from being slowed by noisy neighbours
explain: Tenant isolation and device access come from the hypervisor. The only thing the inner split still buys is protecting the guest kernel from the single application. In a unikernel, a compromised application owns the whole VM, but the VM is all it can reach; this tradeoff comes back in lesson 7.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory
question: Mirage seals a unikernel so no page table changes are allowed after start of day. Which consequence must the application live with?
options: It cannot receive network packets
It must pre-allocate all the memory it needs at startup, since the heap cannot grow by mapping new pages
It cannot use a garbage collector
It must run with a single vCPU
explain: The paper states a sealed VM cannot expand its heap and must pre-allocate its memory at boot; allocation within the heap and I/O mappings still work. The single vCPU in Mirage is a separate design choice, not a consequence of sealing.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: The spectrum: Linux-based unikernels, microVMs and sandboxes
question: A team needs fork, strace and a shell for its service, but wants VMs that boot in tens of milliseconds and strong tenant isolation. Which option fits best?
options: A Unikraft image in binary-compatibility mode
A MirageOS rewrite
A specialized minimal Linux kernel (Lupine-style Kconfig) on a lightweight VMM such as Firecracker
gVisor, because it is the fastest to boot of all VMs
explain: fork and strace need real Linux. A Kconfig-specialized Linux on a lightweight VMM booted in 23 ms in Lupine's evaluation and keeps hardware isolation. Unikraft offers vfork plus execve but no copying fork; MirageOS is OCaml only; gVisor is a user-space kernel, not a VM.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
question: In the toy timeline, miss latency is 100 ns and a distance is 50 ns. Which change helps most?
options: Prefetching two or more neighbors ahead instead of one
Using AVX-512 to halve the 50 ns distance
Removing the visited-array check
Making the neighbor list longer
explain: The CPU waits because each load is issued only one distance (50 ns) before it is needed, but takes 100 ns. Issuing loads earlier overlaps more of the latency. Halving the compute time would make the stall share even larger.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Quickstart, end to end: data, reward, launch, logs and export
question: You rerun the quickstart with a new trainer.experiment_name and the default resume_mode. Where does it start?
options: From the latest checkpoint of the previous experiment
From step 435, because total_epochs is unchanged
It fails because resume_mode requires resume_from_path
From step 1: auto looks only in this experiment's checkpoint directory, which is empty
explain: default_local_dir is checkpoints/<project>/<experiment>, so a new experiment name points auto at an empty directory and training starts fresh. To continue another run, use resume_mode=resume_path with trainer.resume_from_path set to its global_step folder.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: The V1 trainer: TransferQueue, sync and async modes, partial rollout
question: A 32B DAPO run has long-tail response lengths, and your cluster cannot be split evenly between rollout and training nodes: any fixed split leaves one side idle. Which V1 setting fits best?
options: sync with a larger rollout.n
colocate_async with num_warmup_batches=0
separate_async with hybrid_rollout.enable_switch=True
separate_async with max_off_policy_threshold=null
explain: The doc's table names exactly this case for switching: it reduces trainer idle time when it is hard to set a perfect rollouter-to-trainer ratio, because trainer GPUs lend rollout replicas while they would otherwise wait. Removing the staleness bound does not fix the split, and sync keeps waiting for the tail.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Why an hour of video does not fit: frames times tokens
question: Which statement about 8-frame uniform sampling of a 1-hour video is correct?
options: It is fine because the vision encoder sees all frames before sampling
It costs 8 x 196 = 1,568 visual tokens but leaves 7.5-minute gaps the model never sees
It is equivalent to 1 fps sampling with 2 x 2 pooling
It fails only because the LLM context is too short
explain: Sampling happens before the encoder, so unsampled frames are never encoded. 3,600 s / 8 = 450 s between samples. The context is not the issue at 1,568 tokens; the missing information is.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks
question: A support team asks many questions about the same 2-hour screen recording, often about exact error codes shown briefly on screen. Which design fits best?
options: 8 uniformly sampled frames with 2 x 2 pooling
Caption retrieval over 5-second clips alone, since captions are cheap
Index the clips once, retrieve candidate moments per question, then re-inspect those frames at full resolution with a VLM
MovieChat global mode with a 256-frame long-term memory
explain: Many questions favor a reusable index. Brief, small on-screen text is exactly what pooling, merging and generic captions lose, so the retrieved moments need a full-resolution second look.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: The dynamics model: next-frame tokens with MaskGIT
question: Why does Genie train the dynamics model with masking rates drawn between 0.5 and 1 rather than always masking just the last frame completely?
options: To make training cheaper by skipping tokens
Because MaskGIT decoding starts from a heavily masked frame and refines partially filled ones, so training must cover many masking levels
To hide the latent actions from the model
To make the tokenizer's codebook smaller
explain: At inference each frame goes from fully masked to fully filled through intermediate states. Training on a range of masking rates teaches the model to predict masked tokens from the partial context it will see at every iteration.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: VT-x and AMD-V: VM entries, VM exits and the control structure
question: In the toy, the guest passes rax = -1. Why is the vulnerable handler's quiet success more dangerous than the crash at rax = 7?
options: It runs a handler the guest was not meant to reach, with no error to alert anyone; in C it would read memory outside the table
Negative numbers are always rejected by the CPU
It is not dangerous, because hc_log is harmless
Python converts -1 to 0, so the first handler runs
explain: A crash is loud. A wrong-but-silent lookup is how out-of-bounds reads become control of a function pointer. In C, table[-1] reads whatever sits just before the table.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: A toy emulated device: the bounds bug, the fix, and a fuzzer
question: Why did only READ_ID trigger the overflow in the vulnerable ToyFIFO, while ECHO did not?
options: READ_ID has more parameters than the FIFO holds
ECHO is rejected as unknown
ECHO's handler resets pos when its parameters are complete; READ_ID defers the reset to a timer, so further guest bytes keep incrementing pos
READ_ID writes to the DMA base by design
explain: The bug is the combination of an unchecked index and one code path that delays the reset. That is the same shape as VENOM, where most of the 32 FDC command handlers reset the position immediately but two did not.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Case: Hyper-V's vmswitch, and how to read a hypervisor advisory
question: CVE-2021-28476 usually led to a host crash rather than code execution. Why was it still scored 9.9?
options: A guest could crash the host (every tenant down) over a network-reachable path with low privileges, scope changed, and reads of device registers could have further side effects
Because Microsoft scores all Hyper-V bugs as critical
Because it was exploited in the wild
Because the bug was in a user-mode process
explain: The vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H. The scope change (guest to host) and the high impact ratings drive the score. MSRC listed it as not exploited, 'Exploitation Less Likely'.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Attestation: proving what is running before you send it secrets
question: Why does a SEV-SNP verifier reject reports with POLICY bit 19 set, even when the measurement is correct?
options: Bit 19 means SMT is enabled
Bit 19 marks an old report format
Bit 19 means the VCEK was not used
Bit 19 is DEBUG: the firmware's debug commands could then decrypt guest memory for the host, undoing the confidentiality the verifier is relying on
explain: The ABI spec defines bit 19 as DEBUG, and the firmware's SNP_DBG_DECRYPT command only works when the guest's policy allows debugging. A debuggable confidential VM is not confidential.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
question: After loading a 224 checkpoint, you fine-tune at 384 but forget `interpolate_pos_encoding=True` in Hugging Face. What happens?
options: Training silently runs at 224 because the processor crops
The model interpolates anyway, the flag only changes the method
It fails: the 197-row position table does not fit a 577-token sequence
Accuracy is identical, because position embeddings matter little
explain: Without the flag, the Hugging Face embedding layer checks the input size and raises a ValueError (input 384*384 does not match model 224*224); the 197-row table could not be added to 577 tokens anyway. Interpolation happens only when you ask for it.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Binning: one 7-DoF action becomes seven tokens
question: Your dataset has a few teleoperation glitches with huge rotation values. Training with min-max bounds, the robot's wrist motions become jerky and imprecise. What is the most likely cause?
options: The glitches widened the interval, so normal rotations share very few, very wide bins
The LLM's vocabulary is too small to hold 256 tokens
Cross-entropy cannot be used for rotation dimensions
Binning rotations requires 512 bins by definition
explain: Outliers set the min and max, so the bin width grows and most real actions collapse into a handful of bins. This is exactly why OpenVLA bins between the 1st and 99th percentiles.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Why a transformer wants an image as a few discrete tokens
question: A tokenizer downsamples 256 x 256 images by f = 8 instead of f = 16. How long is the token sequence the transformer must model?
options: 256 tokens, because the codebook size is unchanged
1024 tokens, a 32 x 32 grid
512 tokens, because halving f doubles the length
65,536 tokens, one per pixel
explain: Each side shrinks by f, so the grid is (256/8) x (256/8) = 32 x 32 = 1024 tokens. Halving f doubles each side and therefore quadruples the token count, and the number of attention pairs grows 16x.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: FSQ and LFQ: quantizers with no learned codebook
question: Which statement about LFQ with 18 latent dimensions is correct?
options: It stores a 262,144 x 256 embedding table and searches it each step
Each token id is an 18-bit number read off the signs of the latent dimensions
It needs the VQ-VAE codebook loss to keep codes from collapsing
Two vectors with the same signs but different magnitudes get different ids
explain: LFQ quantizes each dimension to sign(z_i) and reads the id as a binary number, so 18 dimensions give 2^18 ids with no table to search. Magnitudes are discarded, and the codebook loss is inapplicable; usage is encouraged by an entropy penalty instead.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
question: On an A100 (compute capability 8.0) you start a BF16 model with `--attention-backend FLASHMLA`. The model is not MLA. What happens?
options: vLLM ignores the flag and uses FLASH_ATTN, the first valid entry
Startup fails with a ValueError listing reasons such as compute capability not supported and non-MLA not supported
FLASHMLA runs, but more slowly than FLASH_ATTN
vLLM switches to TRITON_MLA because it accepts any GPU
explain: An explicit backend is validated alone. FLASHMLA reports `is_mla()` as true and accepts only capability 9.x or 10.x, so `validate_configuration` returns reasons and `get_attn_backend_cls` raises. The design doc shows this same error format.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: FP8 KV caches inside the backends: scales, kernels, support
question: H100, Llama-3-8B in BF16, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e5m2`, no backend pinned. Which backend serves it?
options: FLASH_ATTN, with keys converted to E4M3 on the fly
TRITON_ATTN, because only Triton handles E5M2 on Hopper
Startup fails: no CUDA backend supports E5M2
FLASHINFER, the next entry in the priority list, because FLASH_ATTN never accepts E5M2
explain: `flash_attn_supports_kv_cache_dtype` returns False for fp8_e5m2, so FLASH_ATTN is invalid. FLASHINFER is priority 2 on non-10.x GPUs and lists fp8_e5m2, so it wins. TRITON_ATTN would also be valid, but it comes third.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
question: Qwen2-VL's model card says the default visual-token range is 4 to 16,384 per image and suggests setting max_pixels to 1280 x 28 x 28 to save memory. What happens to a 12-megapixel phone photo under that setting?
options: It is resized, keeping its aspect ratio, so that it fits the pixel budget, and costs about 1,230 tokens instead of about 15,500
It is rejected because it exceeds max_pixels
It is cut into 336 x 336 tiles and every tile is kept
Nothing changes because Qwen2-VL uses native resolution
explain: The resize rule scales the image down, preserving aspect ratio, until it fits within max_pixels, then rounds each side to a multiple of 28. A 3024 x 4032 photo becomes 840 x 1148: 1,230 merged tokens plus 2 markers. Native resolution only holds inside the configured pixel range.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
question: Why does a failed compare&swap make the consensus protocol work for any number of processes, while a lost test&set does not?
options: CAS is faster than test&set on modern hardware
CAS uses more memory, so it can store all inputs
test&set is not atomic
A failed CAS returns the stored value, which is the winner's input; a lost test&set returns only a bit
explain: The losers' problem is identifying the winner. CAS writes the winner's value into the shared word and hands it back to every loser. test&set returns 1 to every loser and carries no identity.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
question: A 0.25 degree latitude-longitude grid covers 90N to 90S. Why does it have 721 rows instead of 720?
options: Because ERA5 adds one row of padding for convolutions
Because both poles are grid rows, so there are 720 intervals and 721 edges
Because the equator is stored twice, once per hemisphere
Because 721 is required to make the grid divisible by 4
explain: 180 degrees divided by 0.25 gives 720 intervals; counting the endpoints 90N and 90S gives 721 rows. Longitude wraps around, so 0 and 360 are the same column and there are exactly 1440.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Uncertainty: GenCast's diffusion ensembles and CRPS
question: Why does GenCast start each forecast step from fresh noise rather than from the previous step's output plus a small perturbation?
options: Diffusion models cannot accept conditioning inputs
Sampling from noise each step lets the model draw a new plausible state from the learned conditional distribution, giving sharp, distinct members
Noise makes the model run faster on TPUs
It removes the need for ERA5 initial conditions
explain: The diffusion model represents p(X(t+1) given X(t), X(t-1)). Each fresh noise draw yields a different sample of that distribution, so trajectories diverge realistically. The previous states still enter as conditioning, and forecasts still start from ERA5 plus perturbations.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: The intercepting proxy: Burp Suite and ZAP as a workflow
question: Which proxy feature is safe to leave running against a bounty target while you browse normally?
options: Passive scanning of the traffic you already send
Active scan
Intruder with a large wordlist
An automated crawler at maximum speed
explain: Passive scanning only reads the requests and responses you already generate; ZAP describes it as not changing the messages and safe to use. Active scans, Intruder runs and fast crawls send new traffic that the policy may forbid.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authentication: enumeration, lockout, reset and skipped steps
question: After entering a password, an app redirects to /mfa. You request /account directly instead and get your account page. Which WSTG test does this fall under?
options: WSTG-ATHN-04 bypassing the authentication schema
WSTG-ATHN-03 lockout
WSTG-SESS-02 cookie attributes
WSTG-IDNT-04 account enumeration
explain: Skipping a step by calling a later page directly is the forced-browsing case WSTG-ATHN-04 describes. The fix is a server-side check of authentication state on every protected page.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Blind SSRF, out-of-band checks and server-side browsers
question: Burp Collaborator records an HTTP request from the target's servers after you submit a webhook URL. What have you shown so far?
options: That the server fetches attacker-supplied URLs, which may be intended; impact depends on what else it can reach
A critical SSRF
Remote code execution
Nothing, since external requests are normal
explain: PortSwigger notes an external interaction doesn't always indicate a vulnerability. For a webhook it is the feature. The finding needs impact: reaching internal services, reading responses, or bypassing a restriction.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Writing a report that gets triaged, fixed and paid
question: A programme scores your finding lower than you expected. What is the most effective response?
options: Explain, on the report, the specific impact or CVSS metric you think was misjudged, with evidence, and accept the final decision
Publish the bug to pressure them
Open a support ticket with the company
Submit the same bug again as a new report
explain: Programmes like GitLab let reporters raise concerns about a metric on the report itself, while the final decision rests with them. Going around the report, publishing or resubmitting breaks the rules.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The same-origin policy: what it blocks and what it lets through
question: Which statement about the same-origin policy is true?
options: It applies only to https pages
It stops script injected into your own pages from reading your cookies
It keeps localStorage separate per origin
It prevents other sites from sending POST requests to your server
explain: Storage such as localStorage and IndexedDB is partitioned by origin. SOP does not stop cross-origin writes such as form POSTs, does nothing against script running inside your origin (XSS), and applies to http and https alike.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: CORS with credentials, and the misconfigurations that leak data
question: An API trusts any origin that fully matches the regular expression `https://.*example\.com`. Which origin would it wrongly trust?
options: https://app.example.com
http://app.example.com
https://hackersexample.com
https://example.com
explain: The .* before example.com matches any characters, including none and including no dot, so hackersexample.com matches. The http origin fails because the pattern requires https. Exact comparison against a list avoids both mistakes.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: HTTPS, mixed content and HSTS: keeping the network out
question: A site sends `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000` in a response served over plain HTTP. What does the browser do?
options: Upgrades this one response to HTTPS
Stores it but only for the current session
Ignores the header, because HSTS is only accepted over HTTPS
Stores the host as HSTS for a year
explain: Browsers ignore HSTS sent over HTTP. Otherwise a MitM could inject a header for a site that does not support HTTPS (locking users out) or strip and replace it. The header must arrive over a secure connection to count.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The map: which bug class gets around which rule
question: Which pairing of bug class and the rule it gets around is correct?
options: Clickjacking gets around CSP script-src
postMessage bugs are fixed by HSTS
Firesheep got around Site Isolation
CORS misconfiguration is a server telling the browser to relax the same-origin policy for the wrong origin
explain: A CORS misconfiguration is the site itself switching off SOP's read protection for origins it should not trust. Clickjacking abuses embedding (fixed by framing headers), Firesheep abused unencrypted transport (fixed by HTTPS, Secure and HSTS), and postMessage bugs need code fixes.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no
question: Which of these is a privilege (in the token) rather than a permission (in an object's DACL)?
options: Read access on the Reports folder for the Sales group
Deny Write on a registry key for Guests
Full control on a service for Administrators
Debug programs (SeDebugPrivilege)
explain: Privileges such as SeDebugPrivilege are listed in the access token and apply across the system. The others are ACEs on particular objects.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: LSASS: why attackers dump its memory, and how Windows protects it
question: A server was fully patched against EternalBlue, yet NotPetya still infected it. According to CISA, what is the most likely route?
options: A zero-day in NTFS
Clearing the Security log
A UAC prompt the admin accepted
Credentials stolen from LSASS on another machine, then used with PsExec or WMIC
explain: CISA describes credential theft with a modified Mimikatz plus PsExec or WMIC as NotPetya's first and most effective method. Patches do not stop valid credentials.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Sysmon and Microsoft Defender: deeper telemetry, built-in defence
question: You want to know which program opened lsass.exe at 02:10 last night. Which source is designed for that?
options: Security event 4720
Defender event 5007
System event 7045
Sysmon event 10 (ProcessAccess)
explain: Sysmon's ProcessAccess event records one process opening another, and Microsoft's documentation names reading LSASS memory as the use case. It needs a config that includes it, with filters for noise.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: First look at domains and Active Directory
question: Why do attackers who land on one workstation in a domain usually aim for Domain Admins rather than staying local?
options: Local admin rights do not exist in a domain
Domain Admins accounts have no SID
Kerberos is turned off for local accounts only
Domain Admins members can control every machine in the domain, so one account gives the whole network
explain: Domain Admins (RID 512) can administer every domain-joined machine and the DCs. Getting there turns one foothold into control of the organisation.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing
question: An attacker has recorded one WPA2-Personal handshake. Which defence actually slows their offline guessing?
options: Turning on the AP's lockout after 5 failed logins
Hiding the SSID
Having chosen a passphrase with many more bits of randomness
Rebooting the AP
explain: Offline guessing never touches the AP, so lockouts and reboots do nothing, and the SSID is already in the recording. Only the size of the space the passphrase was drawn from, and the per-guess cost, set the attacker's time.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: KRACK and FragAttacks: when the standard itself is wrong
question: Why does reinstalling an in-use key break CCMP's security, even though the key itself stays secret?
options: It disables the MIC
The reinstall reveals the key on the air
It resets the packet counter used as the nonce, so frames are encrypted under the same key and nonce again, repeating keystream
It downgrades CCMP to WEP
explain: CCMP (like any counter-mode scheme) is safe only while key and nonce pairs never repeat. Resetting the counter to 1 under the same key repeats them. It is the same keystream reuse that broke WEP in lesson 2.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: iOS: code signing, sandbox, Secure Enclave and BlastDoor
question: Why did Apple add exponential restart throttling to BlastDoor and imagent?
options: Because Swift crashes more often
To save battery
Because many zero-click exploits need to crash a service many times (for example to break ASLR); doubling the restart delay stretches minutes into hours
To stop spam
explain: Project Zero's analysis: crash-oracle techniques learn memory layout by repeatedly crashing a service. With delays doubling up to about 20 minutes, such an exploit would need hours to roughly half a day.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app networking: cleartext, certificate checks and pinning
question: Why does Android's pinning documentation insist on a backup pin?
options: To allow user CAs
To double the encryption strength
Because if the pinned key must change (key rotation or a CA change), an app with only one pin cannot connect until users install an update
Because Android requires exactly two pins
explain: A pin is a hard rule in shipped code. If the server key changes and no other pinned key matches, every installed copy fails closed. A pre-generated backup key, pinned in advance, keeps you able to rotate.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
question: A pool runs 8 workers on 2 microseconds tasks, and its single locked queue costs 0.5 microseconds of serialized work per task. Using the lesson's model, about how many workers can the queue keep busy?
options: All 8, since 2 us tasks are much longer than 0.5 us
About 5, since (s + c)/c = 2.5/0.5 = 5
About 2, since only one thread can hold the lock
About 4, since half the time is spent in the queue
explain: The queue hands out at most 1/c = 2 tasks per microsecond, and each worker consumes 1/(s+c) = 0.4 tasks per microsecond, so the queue saturates at 2/0.4 = 5 workers. The other 3 mostly wait on the lock.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
question: A Tokio runtime has 8 workers and 4 of them are currently searching. A fifth idle worker tries to start searching. What happens?
options: It starts searching; there is no limit
It wakes all other parked workers first
It is refused, because 2 x 4 >= 8, so it goes back to parking
It steals from the global queue only
explain: transition_worker_to_searching returns false when 2 x num_searching >= num_workers, so at most about half the workers search at once. Tokio calls the limit sloppy on purpose: it is a throttle, not an exact bound.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Tuning the cooldown: length, shape, floor and data
question: Why can 1-sqrt beat linear for the same cooldown length?
options: It reaches low LR earlier in the cooldown, giving more steps for the bouncing to settle, at the cost of a little river progress
It keeps the LR near peak for longer during the cooldown
It never reaches zero, so the model keeps learning
It is identical to cosine to 10%
explain: Halfway through the cooldown 1-sqrt is at 0.293 of peak versus 0.5 for linear. Its average LR over the cooldown is 1/3 versus 1/2, so it gives up some area (river progress) in exchange for more time at small LR to shrink the hill part.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
question: A server reads each file with read() into a 64 KiB buffer, then write()s it to a TCP socket. Hot files are always in the page cache. Which costs does the read/write loop add that an in-kernel transfer would avoid?
options: The DMA from disk into the page cache
Two CPU copies per byte and two system calls per chunk
The DMA from the socket buffer to the NIC
Nothing: the page cache already makes it zero-copy
explain: With hot files there is no disk DMA at all, and the NIC DMA is needed by every method. What the loop adds is the copy page cache to user buffer, the copy user buffer to socket buffer, and a read plus a write per chunk. The page cache avoids disk reads, not memory copies.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: When zero-copy pays: measurements, limits and choices
question: Kafka serves fetches with sendfile. A cluster enables TLS between clients and brokers. What happens to the zero-copy path?
options: Kafka stops using sendfile, since TLS runs in user space and the bytes must be encrypted there
Nothing, sendfile encrypts automatically
sendfile switches to splice
The broker uses MSG_ZEROCOPY instead
explain: Kafka's design docs say sendfile is not used when SSL is enabled, because the TLS library lives in user space. Kernel TLS can restore an in-kernel path, but encryption still reads every byte unless a NIC offloads it.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds
question: An auto-tagger publishes tags without human review, and a wrong tag is costly while a missing tag is cheap. How should you set the threshold?
options: Use 0.5, since the scores are probabilities
Pick the threshold that maximizes recall
Use multi_label=False and always take the top label
On a labeled dev set, pick the lowest threshold that reaches the precision target, then confirm on a held-out test split
explain: When false positives are expensive, you constrain precision and take as much recall as that allows. 0.5 has no special meaning for these scores (T3 complaint scored 0.574 and was wrong). Always taking the top label guarantees a tag even when none applies.
